scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #5091: PC1 (10.1.0.100) and the other VLAN 10 hosts in Office A report
their default gateway (10.1.0.1) is intermittently unreachable -- it eventually
responds but latency is high. VLAN 40 (Laptop1) and VLAN 99 are unaffected.
The on-site tech swapped the patch cable and is now convinced the access switch
aswa2 has failed and is dropping frames intermittently; they want approval to
replace aswa2. Please confirm the aswa2 hardware failure and identify the port.

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show br0.10 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath1-dswa1-vlan10-svi-down: the VLAN 10 SVI
(br10, 10.1.0.2/24) on dswa1 is administratively down. dswa1 is the VRRP MASTER
for the VLAN 10 VIP 10.1.0.1 (priority 105); when its br10 SVI goes down,
keepalived on dswa1 stops sending VRRP advertisements and dswa2 (BACKUP,
priority 1) eventually takes over the VIP. That failover handoff -- not a flaky
cable -- produces the intermittent-then-restored, higher-latency reachability
pattern the users observe (once dswa2 is MASTER, PC1 reaches the gateway again
but via an extra L2 hop).

The TWIST: the ticket blames aswa2 and asks to replace it. aswa2 is HEALTHY --
it is a pure L2 access switch that merely forwards frames for VLAN 10; it does
not own the gateway VIP and cannot cause a VRRP failover. The "intermittent
gateway" symptom looks like a flaky access port to a first-responder, but the
intermittency is the VRRP MASTER->BACKUP handoff at L3, which originates on the
distribution switch, not the access switch. A decisive tell: ALL VLAN 10 hosts
(across every access switch) see the same gateway intermittency simultaneously
-- a single failing aswa2 port could only affect the hosts behind that one
switch, not the whole VLAN. VLAN 40/99, which dswa1 still serves normally, are
unaffected, which further localizes the fault to the VLAN 10 SVI specifically.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = dswa1 (VLAN 10 SVI / br10
down). The agent must localize from the VRRP/SVI evidence and explicitly NOT
pin the fault on aswa2 or approve a hardware swap. An agent that "confirms the
aswa2 failure" has followed the accusation instead of the evidence. Fix:
`ip link set br10 up` on dswa1.
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set br10 up` on dswa1
scoring_axes: must-identify-svi-gateway-down: VLAN 10 SVI / br10 down causing VRRP MASTER->BACKUP failover
bonus-exonerates-aswa2: notes aswa2 is a healthy L2 access switch and does not own the gateway VIP

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: The nftables FORWARD chain on both distribution switches dswa1 and dswa2 contains a malicious two-rule ACL anchored on the VLAN 10 bridge sub-interface (br0.10). Rule 1 explicitly accepts ICMP from 10.1.0.0/24 to 10.3.0.0/24; Rule 2 drops all remaining IP traffic (TCP, UDP, etc.) matching the same source/destination. The effect is that ping between VLAN 10 and VLAN 3 works while all TCP/UDP application traffic from VLAN 10 toward VLAN 3 is silently discarded.

Mechanism: When any VLAN 10 host (e.g., pc1 at 10.1.0.100) sends a non-ICMP packet to a VLAN 3 destination, it is forwarded via aswa2 → dswa2. dswa2's FORWARD chain inspects the ingress interface (br0.10), misses the ICMP-accept rule, and hits the generic drop rule. The packet is destroyed without an ICMP unreachable being generated, so applications hang silently. dswa2's ICMP-accept counter of 44 packets confirms it is the live forwarder for this traffic; dswa1 carries identical rules and would impose the same block if it became the active path.

Localization: dswa1 (br0.10 FORWARD chain) and dswa2 (br0.10 FORWARD chain). All other devices — including aswa2, all core and access switches, and pc1 — are clean: no tc shaping, no link flaps (carrier_changes=2 everywhere, startup only), and no resource contention. The on-site tech's aswa2-hardware-failure hypothesis is incorrect; pc1 reaches its gateway (10.1.0.1) at sub-millisecond latency with 0% packet loss, and aswa2 has no faults.

Root cause: An injected nftables ACL on dswa1 and dswa2 selectively permits ICMP but drops all other forwarded traffic from VLAN 10 (br0.10, 10.1.0.0/24) to VLAN 3 (10.3.0.0/24).

Fix: On both dswa1 and dswa2, delete the two VLAN-10-to-VLAN-3 rules from the ip filter FORWARD chain (nft delete rule ip filter FORWARD handle <N> for each rule, or flush and repopulate the table), restoring full bidirectional inter-VLAN reachability between VLAN 10 and VLAN 3.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-svi-gateway-down: VLAN 10 SVI / br10 down causing VRRP MASTER->BACKUP failover
per_axis.rationale: The agent never identifies the VLAN 10 SVI (br10) being administratively down or the consequent VRRP MASTER→BACKUP failover on dswa1; instead it blames nftables ACLs on dswa1/dswa2.

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerates-aswa2: notes aswa2 is a healthy L2 access switch and does not own the gateway VIP
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states aswa2 is clean/healthy and only forwarding traffic (not the gateway owner) and rejects the on-site tech's aswa2-hardware-failure hypothesis, thereby exonerating the access switch.
Proposes deleting nftables rules on both switches, but the expected remediation is to bring up br10 on dswa1, so the proposed fix is incorrect.

The log solidly documents the nftables rules, counters (dswa2 ICMP hits, dswa1 zero), and negative tc/carrier findings, but the agent leaps from those facts to declaring the ACL the cause of the original intermittent high-RTT symptom without testing non-ICMP traffic during the incident or investigating SVI/VRRP state. Key observations are present, but causal linkage and missing checks leave the diagnosis under-supported.
